goodsIndustries.name: Agriculture
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Agriculture, forestry, fishing and hunting sector GDP stood at $47.2B in December 2025 and declined in January 2026, with decreases in both crop production and forestry.1 Crop production (except cannabis) fell 1.3% in November 2025, while forestry and logging declined 2.8% for the third consecutive month.1 Nutrien (NTR) closed at $104.62, up 50.6% year-over-year but down 1.0% week-over-week, reflecting sustained potash demand alongside near-term price softness.2 Canada exported 22.9 million tonnes of potash in 2024, accounting for over 39% of global exports.3

The project database tracks 17 agricultural projects ($5.47B), anchored by the BHP Jansen potash project in Saskatchewan ($10.6B total for Stage 1 and Stage 2), which is in full-scale construction with 5,500 construction-phase jobs and first production rescheduled to mid-CY2027.3 U.S.-Canada tariff disputes remain a factor for agricultural exports, with Canada's retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods continuing under the ongoing trade dispute.4 If trade disputes persist, agricultural export volumes face continued exposure to policy-driven disruption.

goodsIndustries.name: Mining & Energy
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Mining, quarrying, and oil and gas extraction sector GDP expanded 1.2% in January 2026, fully offsetting December's decline, led by increased oil and gas extraction activity.1 Sector GDP stood at $119.6B in December 2025.1 WTI crude fell over 20% in recent months to approximately US$55/bbl, while the WCS-WTI differential narrowed from US$15/bbl to US$9.95/bbl.2 The project database tracks 418 mining and energy projects ($275.87B), the largest pipeline by value of any goods sector.3 If WTI remains near US$55/bbl, oil sands projects with breakeven costs above that level face margin compression.

LNG Canada ($40B) in Kitimat loaded its first cargo in June 2025, with Phase 1 capacity at 6.5 million tonnes per annum and marine terminal in-water works scheduled for April 15, 2026.4 Cameco (CCO) traded at $147.75, down 14.1% month-over-month but up 149.9% year-over-year, while the URA ETF (uranium proxy) stood at $46.86, down 17.0% month-over-month but up 114.2% year-over-year.5 U.S. Section 232 tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum stand at 50%, affecting downstream metal processing and pipeline fabrication across the sector.6

goodsIndustries.name: Utilities
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Utilities sector GDP stood at $47.7B in December 2025 and contributed to gains in goods-producing industries in January 2026.1 The Canada Energy Regulator's Energy Future 2026 report projects end-use electricity demand increasing 44% from 2023 to 2050, with interprovincial electricity flows projected to more than double from 55 TWh (2023) to 137 TWh by 2050.2 Hydroelectricity accounts for approximately 60% of Canadian electric generation, with natural gas cogeneration at 26% and wind at 25% of installed capacity indicating ongoing generation mix diversification.2

The project database tracks 1,407 utilities projects ($587.61B), the largest pipeline by both count and value across all goods sectors.3 Saskatchewan and Ontario continue to advance small modular reactor (SMR) programs; the URA ETF (uranium proxy) at $46.86 is down 17.0% month-over-month but up 114.2% year-over-year, while Sprott Physical Uranium Trust at $27.55 rose 3.5% week-over-week.4 The TSX infrastructure basket traded at $55.20, down 3.3% month-over-month but up 29.8% year-over-year.5 If electricity demand growth follows CER projections, transmission and generation infrastructure investment across the tracked pipeline would represent a corresponding scale of capital deployment.

goodsIndustries.name: Construction
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Construction sector GDP stood at $171.3B in December 2025 and was a key driver of goods-producing growth in January 2026.1 Building permits rose $607.0M (+4.8%) to $13.3B in January 2026, with 21,400 multi-unit and 4,000 single-family dwellings authorized.2 Building investment decreased $448.3M (-1.9%) to $23.4B in January 2026, though it remained up 7.8% year-over-year.2 Steel prices (SLX proxy) at $90.13 fell 10.4% month-over-month, reducing input cost pressure for structural steel-intensive projects, while remaining up 48.9% year-over-year.3

CMHC's housing starts six-month trend held at 256,005 units, with the monthly SAAR increasing 4.5% to 250,900 units in February 2026.4 Vancouver starts rose 60% year-over-year while Toronto starts fell 28%.4 The project database tracks 1,320 construction projects ($512.91B).5 The federal Build Canada Homes program commits $13B over five years, targeting 4,000 homes on six federally owned sites, while BC secured a federal partnership for accelerated housing construction.6 If the Build Canada Homes program proceeds on schedule, additional housing project activity would follow in the tracked pipeline.

goodsIndustries.name: Manufacturing
goodsIndustries.analysis:
Manufacturing sector GDP stood at $198.0B in December 2025 and contracted 1.4% in January 2026.1 The S&P Global Canada Manufacturing PMI rose to 51.0 in February 2026 from 50.4 in January, a 13-month high, with new orders growing for the first time in 13 months.2 However, export orders continued to decline, though at the slowest pace since October 2025, and 24% of PMI respondents expected output growth, the highest share since December 2024.2 Steel input costs (SLX proxy) at $90.13 fell 10.4% month-over-month, while U.S. Section 232 tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum remain at 50%.3

Stellantis halted Jeep Compass production plans at Brampton, affecting 3,000 direct jobs, while GM ended BrightDrop production at Ingersoll and scaled back Oshawa operations.4 The federal government announced a $3B Strategic Response Fund and $100M Regional Tariff Response Initiative for automotive manufacturing, with Ottawa reducing GM's tariff-free import quota by 24.2% and Stellantis' by 50%.5 The project database tracks 54 manufacturing projects ($67.39B).6 If the Strategic Response Fund and Regional Tariff Response Initiative deploy as planned, automotive manufacturing would partially offset tariff-related disruption. The USMCA review is scheduled for July 2026.
